title: POC Weekly - Latency Tuning / TTFT sync (Rivermark)
summary: Weekly POC check-in to review latency runs and tuning experiments. Reviewed TTFT regressions on long sequences, streaming improvements, kernel selection differences across GPUs, and agreed next steps for scale runs and a focused benchmark. Action items assigned for perf runs, log collection, and security/compliance follow-up for Dedicated deployment.
next_steps: Redwood to run 1k sample requests with sequence cutoffs at 128/256/512 and share percentile latencies (Jordan, due 2028-01-11)
Rivermark to provide production traffic sample payloads and typical prompt distributions (Priya, due 2028-01-08)
Schedule a kernel-level deep dive with Redwood infra team for 2028-01-12 (Maya + Samir)
Exchange security questionnaire answers and SOC2 excerpt (Jordan + Carlos, due 2028-01-13)
action_items: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE): assemble consolidated latency CSV and share S3 link by 2028-01-11
Maya Patel (Redwood SE): run kernel A/B tests on A100 vs H100 for q4 int8 path and post logs by 2028-01-11
Priya Nair (Rivermark): provide 7-day traffic sample and typical prompt length histogram by 2028-01-08
Evan Shaw (Rivermark SRE): enable debug traces for the 50-sample failing requests and upload to shared folder by 2028-01-09
Samir Cho (Redwood): schedule 60m kernel deep dive on 2028-01-12 and invite infra folks
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we got 45 minutes, we'll try to cover the TTFT runs, streaming tweaks and kernel experiments.
[00:08] Carlos Ruiz: Yep, thanks Jordan. Priya and Evan here. Quick note, been seeing a weird tail in p95 for long sequences.
[00:15] Priya Nair: yeah, p95 spikes when sequence > 512, TTFT particularly bad when first token delayed.
[00:22] Maya Patel: right so we ran two configs last week - streaming enabled with continuous batching and streaming off with micro-batching. Initial results: streaming cuts TTFT by ~120-180ms median on short seqs but some variability at longer seqs.
[00:36] Priya Nair: we also saw more jitter on H100 in one of your runs, is that expected?
[00:41] Maya Patel: potentially yes, the H100 kernel scheduler plus our kernel selection can lead to variance; some of that was from the attention kernels we picked - we fell back to a generic matmul path for long attention windows, which increases latency.
[00:53] Evan Shaw: when you say "fell back" - is that automatic? I thought you pin kernels per model.
[00:58] Samir Cho: good question, we do a kernel selection step at load time but runtime will re-evaluate based on seq length heuristics; if the compiled optimized kernel doesn't support the observed length it will use a compatible path. That was likely the case.
[01:12] Carlos Ruiz: could that explain the sudden p95 spikes? We saw TTFT median around 260ms but p95 jumps to 820ms on some runs.
[01:19] Maya Patel: yes, that's consistent - the fallback path can multiply token compute by 2-3x on long sequences. Also KV cache warmup behavior matters - if the prefix isn't cached or streaming handshake delays, TTFT moves.
[01:30] Priya Nair: on the streaming handshake, are we seeing any retries or chunking issues?
[01:34] Maya Patel: minimal retries, more chunk boundary misalignment when prompt has many short instructions. We have a tweak that aligns chunk sizes to model's optimal window, which reduced reassembly delay.
[01:45] Jordan Lee: can you share the concrete numbers from your last run? I pulled the csv earlier - short seqs (<=128) median TTFT 120ms with streaming, 240ms without; for 512 seqs medians 360ms streaming vs 520ms without, but tails p95 820ms in some streaming runs because of kernel fallback.
[02:05] Priya Nair: those numbers match our internal smoke tests. Do you suggest quantizing to int8 to reduce variance?
[02:11] Maya Patel: int8 helps throughput but sometimes increases TTFT slightly due to dequant/quant overhead on first token; overall token throughput improves. For strict TTFT budget we recommend mixed strategy: enable streaming + light quantization (q4 or q5/8) and measure.
[02:26] Carlos Ruiz: we plan to keep 300ms TTFT SLO for frontline assistants. Any chance of meeting that at scale?
[02:31] Jordan Lee: possible - with dedicated capacity, prefix caching, and pinned kernels we can hit median TTFT ~150-200ms for typical prompts. P95 will need attention: pinned kernels and pre-warmed KV caches help.
[02:44] Evan Shaw: about pinned kernels - does Redwood support pinning a kernel variant to a model in Dedicated? We want deterministic perf.
[02:50] Samir Cho: yes, for Dedicated we can pin kernel selection and quantization profile in the model config; that removes runtime fallback. There's a small tradeoff in flexibility.
[02:59] Priya Nair: what's the effort to get pinned kernels? Do we need to compile for our exact lengths?
[03:04] Maya Patel: we'll run a short compile pass with sample seq lengths (128/256/512) and build optimized kernels. It takes a day per kernel variant to validate.
[03:13] Priya Nair: ok. For data - we can share a week of anonymized prompts and length histograms.
[03:18] Jordan Lee: great that's one of the action items. Also curious - you mentioned H100 jitter earlier. Could be scheduler noise on multi-tenant nodes; are you on shared or dedicated right now?
[03:27] Evan Shaw: shared cluster for now, but we can try a small Dedicated pool for the POC.
[03:32] Maya Patel: recommended - Dedicated gives isolation and more consistent SLOs. It also lets us pin kernels and reserve KV cache memory.
[03:41] Carlos Ruiz: cost will go up. we'll need numbers. Can you sketch rough cost delta?
[03:45] Jordan Lee: we'll send a cost delta after we pick target throughput; but historically Dedicated premium is 30-60% depending on GPU type and commitment. We can do a hybrid: critical routes on Dedicated, others on Hosted.
[03:58] Priya Nair: a technical question - when streaming is enabled how do you handle long context stitching - do you stream partial responses and the client reassembles?
[04:06] Samir Cho: yes streaming sends chunked tokens while the backend continues generating; we guarantee in-order token delivery. We add sequence IDs and checksums for reassembly in the SDK, but some of the customer's client code had small hiccups in earlier tests.
[04:20] Evan Shaw: we noticed a small gap where the first token arrived later than expected, looks like a TLS handshake delay on client side?
[04:25] Maya Patel: possible - we saw a 30-50ms additional delay when TLS renegotiation occurred; recommend persistent connections and keepalives.
[04:33] Carlos Ruiz: what about kernel differences across cloud vendors? If we run Dedicated on GCP versus Azure do we expect big changes?
[04:40] Samir Cho: kernel performance is mostly GPU microarchitecture dependent; H100 vs A100 has measurable differences. Also driver versions and MIG settings can alter perf slightly. We'll run across both for apples-to-apples.
[04:52] Priya Nair: can you explain the 'prefix caching' again - we have templates with long system prompts, can that be cached?
[04:58] Maya Patel: yes prefix/KV caching caches the key/value pairs for the common system prompt so subsequent requests with the same prefix skip recomputing keys. That reduces cost and TTFT for repeated patterns. For variable prefixes we use partial caching heuristics.
[05:12] Priya Nair: how do we measure cache hit rate?
[05:15] Jordan Lee: we'll provide logs with a cache_hit boolean per request in the perf CSV. Hit rate target should be >70% for good savings.
[05:22] Carlos Ruiz: security question - for Dedicated, where do logs live, and can we point KMS to our HSM?
[05:29] Jordan Lee: Dedicated supports customer-managed KMS and HSM integration, logs can be shipped to your S3/GCS, and we support role-based access controls. We'll attach the security doc.
[05:38] Priya Nair: ok great. Back to experiments - Maya, can you walk through the kernel A/B plan?
[05:43] Maya Patel: plan is: run 500 sample requests per seq length bucket (128/256/512) across A100 and H100 on both int8 and fp16 paths, compare median and p95 TTFT, and capture kernel selection events. We'll also run a streaming-on vs streaming-off toggle. That should highlight fallback conditions.
[06:02] Evan Shaw: what about compilation time? If we compile pinned kernels for many lengths, that's a lot.
[06:06] Samir Cho: yes, but we usually choose representative buckets from your histogram; avoids explosion. Also incremental compilation works - we can compile on-demand and promote validated kernels to pinned set.
[06:17] Priya Nair: timeline wise - when can we expect the A/B results?
[06:20] Maya Patel: we can run them this week and plan to have consolidated results by 2028-01-11.
[06:25] Jordan Lee: perfect. Let's enumerate the acceptance criteria for this POC phase - Rivermark wants median TTFT <300ms and p95 <600ms on typical traffic. Anything to add?
[06:34] Carlos Ruiz: also deterministic behavior during peak hours and less than 5% request failures.
[06:39] Jordan Lee: noted. We'll focus tests on peak-load runs as well.
[06:42] Priya Nair: ok thanks. Quick note - we found a small mismatch in one of the SDKs where chunk IDs were off by one, caused minor reorders. Will send an issue.
[06:51] Maya Patel: we'll take that. Samir will triage.
[06:55] Jordan Lee: wrap up - action items reviewed, next steps agreed. We'll share the kernel test plan and cost delta. Anything else?
[07:03] Carlos Ruiz: no, thanks all.
[07:06] Jordan Lee: thanks, we'll follow up in thread. Bye.
notes: Meeting had some transcription artifacts; speakers sometimes overlap in transcript. Main decision points: run full A/B kernel tests, provide traffic sample, consider Dedicated for deterministic TTFT, and exchange security docs.
